gifttax.imposition.value: imposed for each calendar year on the transfer of property by gift by any individual, resident or nonresident — but not on a nonresident who is not a citizen transferring intangible property, except as IRC § 2501(a)(3) provides (IRC § 2501(a))

gifttax.death_recomputation.value: in computing the estate tax subtraction for gift tax payable, the rates in effect at death are used in place of the rates in force when the gifts were made, both for the chapter 12 tax and for the IRC § 2505 credit against it (IRC § 2001(g)(1))

gifttax.exclusion_difference_regs.value: the Secretary is directed to prescribe regulations addressing any difference between the basic exclusion amount at the decedent's death and the amount applicable to gifts the decedent made (IRC § 2001(g)(2))

gifteffect.gross_up.value: the gross estate is increased by any gift tax paid by the decedent or the decedent's spouse on gifts made during the 3-year period ending at death — so paying the gift tax does not get that money out of the estate unless the donor survives three years (IRC § 2035(b))

gst.transfers.value: three, and only three — a taxable distribution, a taxable termination and a direct skip (IRC § 2611(a))

gst.skip_person.value: a natural person assigned to a generation 2 or more generations below the transferor's, or a trust in which all interests are held by skip persons or from which no distribution may be made to a non-skip person (IRC § 2613(a))

gst.lineal_assignment.value: for a lineal descendant of a grandparent of the transferor or of the transferor's spouse, generation is assigned by counting generations from that grandparent — by family tree, never by age — with legal adoption treated as blood and the half-blood as the whole-blood (IRC § 2651(b))

gst.age_assignment.value: only for an individual not assigned by the family rules: born not more than 12½ years after the transferor is the transferor's own generation, more than 12½ but not more than 37½ years after is the first younger generation, and a new generation every 25 years after that (IRC § 2651(d))

gst.spouse_assignment.value: anyone who has ever been married to the transferor takes the transferor's own generation, and anyone who has ever been married to a lineal descendant takes that descendant's generation — so a much younger spouse is never a skip person (IRC § 2651(c))

gst.predeceased_parent.value: where a descendant of a parent of the transferor, or of the transferor's spouse or former spouse, has a parent who died before the transfer, that individual and their descendants move up a generation — so a grandchild whose parent has died is not a skip person (IRC § 2651(e))

gst.excluded_transfers.value: a transfer that would not be a taxable gift by reason of IRC § 2503(e), and a transfer already taxed under chapter 13 to a transferee at the same or a lower generation where the transfers do not have the effect of avoiding the tax (IRC § 2611(b))

gst.applicable_rate.value: the maximum federal estate tax rate multiplied by the inclusion ratio — a flat top-bracket rate, not a graduated one, and reduced to nil only by allocating exemption (IRC § 2641(a))

gst.exemption_mechanics.value: every individual has a GST exemption equal to the IRC § 2010(c) basic exclusion amount for the calendar year, allocable by the individual or the executor to property of which they are the transferor, and any allocation once made is irrevocable (IRC § 2631)

form709.who_files.value: any individual making a transfer by gift in a calendar year, except a transfer excluded by IRC § 2503(b) or (e), a transfer deductible under § 2523, and a qualifying entire-interest charitable transfer under § 2522 — so the exclusions decide the filing obligation, not the amount of tax (IRC § 6019)

form709.due_date.value: 15 April following the close of the calendar year (IRC § 6075(b)(1))

form709.automatic_extension.value: an extension of time granted for the donor's calendar-year income tax return is deemed also an extension for the gift tax return — no separate request is needed where a Form 4868 is already in (IRC § 6075(b)(2))

form709.death_year_cutoff.value: for the calendar year that includes the donor's death, the gift tax return is due no later than the time, including extensions, for filing that donor's estate tax return — which is usually earlier than the following 15 April (IRC § 6075(b)(3))

form709.who_pays.value: the donor (IRC § 2502(c)) — and payment is due at the time fixed for filing the return, determined without regard to any extension of time to file (IRC § 6151(a))

form709.no_joint_return.value: there is no joint gift tax return — spouses who split gifts each file their own return and signify consent on it, and consent makes each liable for the entire tax of both for that year (IRC §§ 2513(b), (d))

form709.gst_allocation_time.value: an allocation of GST exemption may be made at any time up to the date prescribed for filing the individual's estate tax return, with extensions, whether or not such a return is required (IRC § 2632(a)(1))

form709.gst_deemed_allocation.value: exemption is allocated automatically to a lifetime direct skip so far as needed to bring the inclusion ratio to zero, unless the individual elects out of that treatment (IRC § 2632(b))

form709.unlimited_assessment.value: where a gift required to be shown on a gift tax return — determined without regard to the annual exclusion — is not shown, the gift tax may be assessed at any time, with no period of limitation, unless the item is disclosed on the return or an attached statement in a manner adequate to apprise the Secretary of its nature (IRC § 6501(c)(9))

intlfile.8938_due.value: attached to the annual income tax return and due on the date of that return, including any applicable extensions — it is not a standalone filing (IRC § 6038D(a); IRS Form 8938 and FBAR comparison)
intlfile.8938_due.source: IRC § 6038D(a), read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6038D, and IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements, irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

intlfile.fbar_due.value: received by 15 April following the calendar year reported, with an automatic 6-month extension to 15 October that need not be requested — filed electronically through FinCEN's BSA E-Filing System and never with a federal tax return
intlfile.fbar_due.source: IRS, Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR), irs.gov, and IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements, irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

intlfile.fbar_valuation.value: the maximum value of each account during the year, taken from periodic account statements in the currency of the account and converted at the end-of-calendar-year exchange rate — the maximum balance, not the closing balance
intlfile.fbar_valuation.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements, irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

intlfile.8938_valuation.value: the maximum value of each specified foreign financial asset, at fair market value in United States dollars in accordance with the Form 8938 instructions, converted at the end-of-taxable-year exchange rate
intlfile.8938_valuation.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements, irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

intlfile.5471_timing.value: furnished for the annual accounting period of the foreign business entity ending with or within the United States person's taxable year, at the time and in the manner the Secretary prescribes — in practice with the income tax return (IRC § 6038(a)(2))

intlfile.3520_event_notice.value: on or before the 90th day after a reportable event, or such later day as the Secretary prescribes — the creation of a foreign trust by a United States person, a transfer of money or property to one including by reason of death, and the death of a citizen or resident in the circumstances the section sets out (IRC § 6048(a))

intlfile.3520a_owner_duty.value: a United States person treated as the owner of any portion of a foreign trust must submit the prescribed information and is responsible for ensuring the trust itself files a return with a full accounting of its activities, names its United States agent, and furnishes information to United States owners and beneficiaries (IRC § 6048(b))

intlfile.foreign_gift_threshold.value: aggregate foreign gifts received by a United States person during the taxable year exceeding $10,000 — a foreign gift being any amount received from a non-United States person that the recipient treats as a gift or bequest, excluding a qualified transfer (IRC § 6039F(a), (b))

intlfile.8938_statutory_floor.value: $50,000 of aggregate value is the figure IRC § 6038D(a) prints, subject to 'such higher dollar amount as the Secretary may prescribe' — the four threshold pairs that actually apply are regulatory, so the section alone understates the requirement for every filer but an unmarried one living in the United States
intlfile.8938_statutory_floor.source: IRC § 6038D(a), read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6038D, and IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements, irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.8938_definition.value: any financial account within IRC § 1471(d)(2) maintained by a foreign financial institution, plus three categories held outside such an account — stock or a security issued by a non-United States person, a financial instrument or contract held for investment with a non-United States issuer or counterparty, and any interest in a foreign entity (IRC § 6038D(b))

covered.fbar_definition.value: a financial interest in, or signature or other authority over, at least one financial account located outside the United States — and generally an account at a financial institution located outside the United States is a foreign financial account, whether or not it produced taxable income
covered.fbar_definition.source: IRS, Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR), irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/report-of-foreign-bank-and-financial-accounts-fbar

covered.branch_rule.value: an account at a foreign branch of a United States institution is reportable on the FBAR but not on Form 8938; an account at a United States branch of a foreign institution is reportable on neither — location of the branch decides the FBAR, and the status of the institution decides Form 8938
covered.branch_rule.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.signature_authority.value: signature authority over an account, without any interest in it, is reportable on the FBAR subject to exceptions but is not a Form 8938 asset unless the filer otherwise has an interest — which is why an employee with authority over a company account can have an FBAR obligation and no tax reporting at all
covered.signature_authority.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.non_account_assets.value: foreign stock or securities held outside an account, foreign partnership interests, and foreign hedge and private equity funds are Form 8938 assets and are not FBAR accounts — the FBAR reaches accounts, Form 8938 reaches assets
covered.non_account_assets.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.contents_not_separate.value: where foreign stock or securities are held in an account at a foreign financial institution, the account is reportable but its contents are not separately reported — on both forms
covered.contents_not_separate.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.indirect_interest.value: an indirect interest in foreign financial assets through an entity is not itself a Form 8938 asset, but gives an FBAR financial interest where the ownership or beneficial interest in the entity is greater than 50 percent
covered.indirect_interest.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.not_reportable.value: neither form reaches foreign real estate held directly, foreign currency held directly, precious metals held directly, personal property held directly such as art, antiques, jewellery, cars and collectibles, or social-security-type benefits provided by a foreign government
covered.not_reportable.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.real_estate_through_entity.value: foreign real estate held through a foreign entity is on neither form directly, but the foreign entity itself is a specified foreign financial asset for Form 8938 and its maximum value includes the value of the real estate
covered.real_estate_through_entity.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.insurance_and_funds.value: a foreign-issued life insurance or annuity contract with a cash value is reportable on both forms, as is a foreign mutual fund — while a domestic mutual fund investing in foreign stocks and securities is reportable on neither
covered.insurance_and_funds.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

covered.grantor_trust.value: foreign accounts and foreign non-account investment assets held by a foreign or domestic grantor trust of which the filer is the grantor are Form 8938 assets as to both, and FBAR accounts as to the foreign accounts
covered.grantor_trust.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

intlpen.8938.value: $10,000 for the failure, and where it continues more than 90 days after the Secretary mails notice, a further $10,000 for each 30-day period or fraction of one after that 90-day period expires — the additional penalty capped at $50,000, so $60,000 is the maximum (IRC § 6038D(d))

intlpen.8938_grace.value: 90 days from the mailing of notice before any additional penalty begins to run — a failure cured inside that window carries the $10,000 base penalty and nothing more (IRC § 6038D(d)(2))

intlpen.fbar_nonwillful.value: a civil money penalty not exceeding $10,000, with no penalty at all where the violation was due to reasonable cause and the balance in the account was properly reported — figures in title 31 are adjusted annually for inflation (31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5)(A), (B))

intlpen.fbar_willful.value: the greater of $100,000 or 50 percent of the balance in the account at the time of the violation, and the reasonable cause exception does not apply (31 U.S.C. § 5321(a)(5)(C), (D))

intlpen.fbar_criminal.value: a fine of up to $250,000 or up to 5 years' imprisonment or both for a willful violation, rising to $500,000 and 10 years where the violation occurs while violating another federal law or as part of a pattern of illegal activity involving more than $100,000 in a 12-month period (31 U.S.C. § 5322(a), (b))

intlpen.6677_trust.value: the greater of $10,000 or 35 percent of the gross reportable amount for a failure under IRC § 6048, reduced to 5 percent for the annual return of a foreign trust with a United States owner, plus $10,000 for each 30-day period after a 90-day grace following notice (IRC § 6677(a), (b))

intlpen.foreign_gift.value: the Secretary determines the tax consequences of the receipt, and the recipient pays 5 percent of the gift for each month the failure continues, capped at 25 percent — subject to a reasonable cause exception (IRC § 6039F(c))

intlpen.6038_credit_reduction.value: a 10 percent reduction of the foreign taxes paid or deemed paid for the year, and where the failure continues 90 days or more after notice, 10 percent plus a further 5 percent for each 3-month period or fraction of one after that — a reduction of tax attributes on top of the dollar penalty (IRC § 6038(c)(1), (2))

intlpen.accuracy_40.value: 40 percent instead of 20 percent on the portion of an underpayment attributable to an undisclosed foreign financial asset — an asset for which information was required under IRC § 6038, 6038B, 6038D, 6046A or 6048 and was not provided (IRC § 6662(j))

intlpen.limitations.value: the assessment period for any tax to which the information relates does not expire before 3 years after the information is actually furnished — reaching failures under IRC §§ 1295(b), 1298(f), 6038, 6038A, 6038B, 6038D, 6046, 6046A and 6048, and confined to the items related to the failure only where it was due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect (IRC § 6501(c)(8))

intlpen.title31_inflation.value: the $10,000 non-willful maximum and the $100,000 willful floor printed in 31 U.S.C. § 5321 are statutory bases adjusted annually for inflation, so the figures in the section are not the operative amounts — the IRS notes on its own FBAR materials that published penalty figures may not be current
intlpen.title31_inflation.source: 31 U.S.C. § 5321, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/31/5321, and IRS, Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR), irs.gov

distinct.who_8938.value: specified individuals — United States citizens, resident aliens and certain non-resident aliens — and specified domestic entities, being certain domestic corporations, partnerships and trusts
distinct.who_8938.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

distinct.who_fbar.value: United States persons, including citizens, resident aliens, trusts, estates and domestic entities, with an interest in foreign financial accounts meeting the threshold
distinct.who_fbar.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

distinct.territories.value: United States territories are outside the United States for Form 8938 but inside it for the FBAR — resident aliens of the territories and territory entities are subject to FBAR reporting, which is the one place the two regimes disagree about what the country is
distinct.territories.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

distinct.threshold_shape.value: Form 8938 uses four threshold pairs varying by filing status and residence, each with a last-day figure and an any-time figure; the FBAR uses one cumulative figure with no last-day test and no variation for status or residence
distinct.threshold_shape.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

distinct.interest_test.value: an interest arises for Form 8938 where any income, gain, loss, deduction, credit, gross proceeds or distribution from the asset would be required to be reflected on the income tax return; for the FBAR it arises from being owner of record or holder of legal title, from that person being the filer's agent, from a sufficient interest in the entity that holds title, or from signature authority
distinct.interest_test.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

distinct.no_substitution.value: neither filing satisfies the other — the same account can be reportable on both, on one, or on neither, and the two are administered by different agencies under different titles of the United States Code
distinct.no_substitution.source: IRS, Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements (page last reviewed 18 September 2025), irs.gov/businesses/comparison-of-form-8938-and-fbar-requirements

cfc.us_shareholder.value: a United States person owning, directly, indirectly or by attribution under IRC § 958, 10 percent or more of the total combined voting power of all voting classes of stock of a foreign corporation, or 10 percent or more of the total value of its stock (IRC § 951(b))

cfc.definition.value: a foreign corporation more than 50 percent of whose voting power or stock value is owned, or considered owned under IRC § 958(b), by United States shareholders on any day during its taxable year (IRC § 957(a))

cfc.net_tested_income.value: each United States shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation includes in gross income their net CFC tested income — the aggregate pro rata share of tested income of each such corporation over the aggregate pro rata share of tested loss (IRC § 951A(a), (b))

cfc.gilti_renamed.value: there is no longer a provision called global intangible low-taxed income — Pub. L. 119-21 § 70323(a) substituted 'net CFC tested income' for 'global intangible low-taxed income' in the catchline and text of IRC § 951A and struck the subsection defining GILTI and the net deemed tangible income return, so the qualified business asset investment offset no longer exists
cfc.gilti_renamed.source: IRC § 951A and its 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/951A

cfc.qbai_repealed.value: repealed — Pub. L. 119-21 § 70323(a)(2) struck IRC § 951A(d), which had defined qualified business asset investment, so the inclusion is no longer reduced by a deemed return on tangible assets held abroad
cfc.qbai_repealed.source: IRC § 951A and its 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/951A

cfc.section_250_deduction.value: 40 percent of the net CFC tested income amount included under IRC § 951A and of the related § 78 gross-up, plus 33.34 percent of foreign-derived deduction eligible income — allowed to a domestic corporation only, and subject to a taxable income limitation (IRC § 250(a))

cfc.section_962_election.value: an individual United States shareholder may elect to have the tax on IRC § 951(a) inclusions computed at corporate rates under § 11 in lieu of §§ 1 and 55, and to be treated as a domestic corporation for the § 960 foreign tax credit — the route by which an individual reaches the corporate-level relief (IRC § 962(a))

cfc.transition_tax.value: a one-time increase to subpart F income for the last taxable year of a deferred foreign income corporation beginning before 1 January 2018, equal to the greater of its accumulated post-1986 deferred foreign income at 2 November 2017 or at 31 December 2017 (IRC § 965(a))

cfc.transition_installments.value: 8 installments if elected — 8 percent of the net tax liability for each of the first five, 15 percent for the sixth, 20 percent for the seventh and 25 percent for the eighth, the first due on the unextended due date of the return for the inclusion year (IRC § 965(h))

cfc.transition_spent.value: spent as an operative charge — IRC § 965(a) reaches only the last taxable year of a deferred foreign income corporation beginning before 1 January 2018, so no new inclusion can arise, and what survives is the § 965(h) installment stream and the compliance history it left behind

vd.willfulness_fork.value: willfulness decides the route — the streamlined procedures require a certification that the failure was non-willful, and the Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice requires the taxpayer to state that the conduct was willful and to sign an acknowledgement of it
vd.willfulness_fork.source: IRS, Streamlined filing compliance procedures, irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/streamlined-filing-compliance-procedures; IRS, IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice, irs.gov/compliance/criminal-investigation/irs-criminal-investigation-voluntary-disclosure-practice

vd.nonwillful_definition.value: conduct due to negligence, inadvertence or mistake, or conduct resulting from a good faith misunderstanding of the requirements of the law

vd.streamlined_eligibility.value: individual taxpayers and estates of individuals only; unavailable once the IRS has begun a civil examination of any taxable year, whether or not it concerns foreign assets, or where the taxpayer is under criminal investigation; a valid taxpayer identification number is required; and penalties previously assessed are not abated

vd.streamlined_periods.value: the most recent 3 years for which the return due date, including any properly applied for extension, has passed, together with all required information returns — and the most recent 6 years for which the FBAR due date has passed
vd.streamlined_periods.source: IRS, U.S. taxpayers residing outside the United States, irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/u-s-taxpayers-residing-outside-the-united-states; IRS, U.S. taxpayers residing in the United States, irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/u-s-taxpayers-residing-in-the-united-states

vd.foreign_terms.value: no failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, accuracy-related, information return or FBAR penalties for a taxpayer meeting the non-residency requirement who complies — and that protection survives a later audit unless the examination determines the original noncompliance was fraudulent or the FBAR violation willful
vd.foreign_terms.source: IRS, U.S. taxpayers residing outside the United States, irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/u-s-taxpayers-residing-outside-the-united-states

vd.domestic_penalty.value: a Title 26 miscellaneous offshore penalty of 5 percent of the highest aggregate balance or value of the foreign financial assets subject to it — found by aggregating year-end balances and values for each year in the 3-year covered tax return period and the 6-year covered FBAR period and taking the highest of those years
vd.domestic_penalty.source: IRS, U.S. taxpayers residing in the United States, irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/u-s-taxpayers-residing-in-the-united-states

vd.domestic_eligibility.value: the taxpayer must fail the non-residency requirement, must have previously filed a return for each of the most recent 3 years for which the due date has passed, must have failed to report gross income from a foreign financial asset, and the failures must have been non-willful
vd.domestic_eligibility.source: IRS, U.S. taxpayers residing in the United States, irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/u-s-taxpayers-residing-in-the-united-states

vd.streamlined_no_closure.value: returns are processed like any other return — receipt is not acknowledged, there is no closing agreement, and the submission may still be selected for audit under the ordinary processes and checked against information received from banks and other sources

vd.vdp_timeliness.value: a disclosure is timely only if received before the IRS has commenced a civil examination or criminal investigation, received information from a third party alerting it to the noncompliance, or acquired information about it from a criminal enforcement action such as a search warrant or grand jury subpoena
vd.vdp_timeliness.source: IRS, IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice, irs.gov/compliance/criminal-investigation/irs-criminal-investigation-voluntary-disclosure-practice

vd.vdp_no_immunity.value: a voluntary disclosure will not automatically guarantee immunity from prosecution — Criminal Investigation takes a timely, accurate and complete disclosure into consideration in deciding whether to recommend prosecution, and it may result in prosecution not being recommended
vd.vdp_no_immunity.source: IRS, IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice, irs.gov/compliance/criminal-investigation/irs-criminal-investigation-voluntary-disclosure-practice

vd.vdp_mechanics.value: a two-part application on Form 14457 — Part I preclearance, which determines eligibility but does not guarantee preliminary acceptance, then Part II within 45 days of the preclearance letter, with at most one 45-day extension; full payment or a full-pay installment agreement for tax, interest and penalties is required
vd.vdp_mechanics.source: IRS, IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice, irs.gov/compliance/criminal-investigation/irs-criminal-investigation-voluntary-disclosure-practice

vd.vdp_illegal_source.value: the practice does not apply to taxpayers with illegal sources of income, and income from activities legal under state law but illegal under federal law is treated as illegal source income for this purpose
vd.vdp_illegal_source.source: IRS, IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice, irs.gov/compliance/criminal-investigation/irs-criminal-investigation-voluntary-disclosure-practice

vd.vdp_proposal_status.value: a proposed revision of the practice was announced on 22 December 2025 for a 90-day comment period ending 22 March 2026 and has not been finalised — the IRS states the proposal creates no rights or expectations for taxpayers who applied before it is finalised and placed into effect, and eligibility under any revised practice will be determined by the procedures in effect when the changes are finalised
vd.vdp_proposal_status.source: IRS, IRS Criminal Investigation Voluntary Disclosure Practice, irs.gov/compliance/criminal-investigation/irs-criminal-investigation-voluntary-disclosure-practice (read 21 August 2026)

soleprop.disregarded.value: a business entity with a single owner that is not a corporation under Reg. § 301.7701-2(b) is disregarded as an entity separate from its owner for federal tax purposes (Reg. § 301.7701-2(c)(2)(i))

soleprop.return_date.value: the same date as the owner's individual return — a sole proprietorship files no return of its own, so the business is reported on a schedule to the Form 1040 and follows the individual calendar in IRC § 6072(a), not the 15 March date that applies to partnerships and S corporations under § 6072(b)

soleprop.se_return_threshold.value: $400 or more of net earnings from self-employment for the taxable year obliges every individual other than a nonresident alien to make a self-employment tax return, and on a joint return the tax is computed on each spouse's separate self-employment income rather than on the aggregate (IRC § 6017)

soleprop.net_earnings.value: gross income derived from any trade or business carried on by the individual, less the deductions attributable to that trade or business, plus the distributive share of income or loss from any trade or business carried on by a partnership of which the individual is a member (IRC § 1402(a))

soleprop.se_floor.value: net earnings from self-employment of less than $400 are excluded from self-employment income altogether — an unindexed figure, so the exclusion has narrowed steadily in real terms (IRC § 1402(b)(2))

soleprop.trade_or_business.value: trade or business for self-employment purposes has the same meaning as in IRC § 162, subject to the exclusions that section 1402(c) then lists (IRC § 1402(c))

soleprop.deduction_standard.value: all the ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business, including reasonable compensation for services actually rendered and travelling expenses that are not lavish or extravagant (IRC § 162(a))

ptr.definition.value: a syndicate, group, pool, joint venture or other unincorporated organization through or by means of which any business, financial operation or venture is carried on, and which is not a corporation, trust or estate (IRC § 761(a); § 7701(a)(2))

ptr.no_entity_tax.value: a partnership as such is not subject to the income tax — persons carrying on business as partners are liable for income tax only in their separate or individual capacities (IRC § 701)

ptr.separately_stated.value: each partner takes into account separately their distributive share of the classes IRC § 702(a) lists — short-term and long-term capital gains and losses, § 1231 gains and losses, charitable contributions, dividends, foreign taxes, other separately stated items, and then the residual taxable income or loss (IRC § 702(a))

ptr.return_requirement.value: every partnership must make a return for each taxable year stating its items of gross income and allowable deductions, with the names and addresses of those entitled to share in the taxable income if distributed (IRC § 6031(a))

ptr.due_date.value: the 15th day of March following the close of a calendar year, or the 15th day of the third month following the close of a fiscal year (IRC § 6072(b))

ptr.late_penalty.value: $260 per partner per month for each month or fraction of one during which the failure continues, capped at 12 months, unless the failure is due to reasonable cause — the statute prints $195 and IRC § 6698(e) indexes it, rounding down to a multiple of $5 (IRC § 6698; Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 3.55, for returns required to be filed in 2027)
ptr.late_penalty.source: IRC § 6698, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6698, and Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 3.55, re-downloaded from irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf and text-extracted 21 August 2026

qjv.effect.value: the venture is not treated as a partnership, all items of income, gain, loss, deduction and credit are divided between the spouses according to their respective interests, and each takes their share into account as if attributable to a trade or business conducted as a sole proprietor (IRC § 761(f)(1))

qjv.conditions.value: three, and only three — the only members are a husband and wife, both materially participate within IRC § 469(h) determined without regard to § 469(h)(5), and both elect the subsection to apply; the election is available only where they file a joint return for the year (IRC § 761(f)(1), (2))

ptr.exclusion_election.value: all the members of an unincorporated organization may elect to exclude it from all or part of subchapter K where it is availed of for investment purposes only and not the active conduct of a business, for the joint production, extraction or use of property but not for selling services or the property produced, or by dealers in the circumstances the section sets out (IRC § 761(a))

corp.rate.value: 21 percent of taxable income — a flat rate with no brackets (IRC § 11(b))

corp.return_date.value: the 15th day of April following the close of a calendar year, or the 15th day of the fourth month following the close of a fiscal year — a C corporation falls under the general rule in IRC § 6072(a), not the third-month rule in § 6072(b) that governs partnerships and S corporations

corp.charitable_limits.value: allowed only to the extent the aggregate exceeds 1 percent of taxable income and does not exceed 10 percent of taxable income — a floor as well as a ceiling, both applying to taxable years beginning after 31 December 2025 (IRC § 170(b)(2)(A) as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70426(a), (d))
corp.charitable_limits.source: IRC § 170(b)(2) and its 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/170

corp.charitable_superseded.value: a single ceiling of 10 percent of taxable income with no floor — the rule for taxable years beginning before 2026, and before that a temporary 25 percent ceiling for certain cash contributions in 2020 and 2021 that has long since lapsed
corp.charitable_superseded.source: IRC § 170(b)(2)(A) and its 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/170

corp.charitable_carryover.value: contributions disallowed by the 10 percent ceiling carry to the succeeding year and expire after the fifth taxable year following the year first taken into account, on a first-in first-out basis — with current-year contributions absorbed before carried amounts, and amounts disallowed by the 1 percent floor carried forward only from a year in which the 10 percent ceiling was also exceeded (IRC § 170(d)(2))

corp.beat_rate.value: 10.5 percent of modified taxable income, less regular tax liability adjusted as IRC § 59A(b)(1)(B) provides — Pub. L. 119-21 § 70331(a)(1) substituted 10.5 percent for 10 percent and § 70331(a)(2) struck the paragraph that would have raised the rate for taxable years beginning after 2025 (IRC § 59A(b)(1))
corp.beat_rate.source: IRC § 59A and its 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/59A

corp.beat_applicable_taxpayer.value: a corporation other than a regulated investment company, real estate investment trust or S corporation, with average annual gross receipts of at least $500,000,000 for the 3 taxable years ending with the preceding year, and a base erosion percentage of 3 percent or higher — 2 percent for a bank or securities dealer (IRC § 59A(e)(1))

corp.capital_losses.value: losses from sales or exchanges of capital assets are allowed only to the extent of gains from such sales or exchanges — a corporation has no equivalent of the individual allowance against ordinary income (IRC § 1211(a))

corp.capital_loss_carry.value: a net capital loss is carried back to each of the 3 preceding taxable years, so far as it does not increase or produce a net operating loss, and forward to each of the 5 succeeding years — treated as a short-term capital loss in each, and carried to the earliest available year first (IRC § 1212(a)(1))

corp.distribution_character.value: the portion of a distribution that is a dividend within IRC § 316 is included in the shareholder's gross income; the rest is applied against and reduces stock basis, and any excess over basis is treated as gain from a sale or exchange (IRC § 301(c))

corp.estimated_required.value: 25 percent of the required annual payment per installment, the required annual payment being the lesser of 100 percent of the tax shown on the current year's return or 100 percent of the tax shown on the preceding year's return — the prior-year branch unavailable where that year was not 12 months or the corporation filed no return showing a liability (IRC § 6655(d)(1))

corp.estimated_de_minimis.value: no addition to tax where the tax shown on the return for the year, or the tax if no return is filed, is less than $500 (IRC § 6655(f))

corp.estimated_large.value: a large corporation may not use the prior-year branch at all, except that it may use last year's tax for the first installment with the shortfall recaptured in the second (IRC § 6655(d)(2))

corp.at_risk.value: the money and adjusted basis of other property contributed to the activity, plus amounts borrowed to the extent the taxpayer is personally liable for repayment or has pledged property not used in the activity as security, to the extent of the net fair market value of that pledged interest (IRC § 465(b)(1), (2))

scorp.eligibility.value: a domestic corporation that is not an ineligible corporation and does not have more than 100 shareholders, does not have a shareholder who is not an individual other than an estate, a qualifying trust or a qualifying exempt organisation, does not have a nonresident alien shareholder, and does not have more than one class of stock (IRC § 1361(b)(1))

scorp.family_aggregation.value: a husband and wife and their estates count as one shareholder, and all members of a family and their estates count as one — a family being a common ancestor, that ancestor's lineal descendants and the spouses and former spouses of either, with the common ancestor no more than 6 generations removed from the youngest generation of shareholders (IRC § 1361(c)(1))

scorp.election_timing.value: at any time during the preceding taxable year, or during the taxable year on or before the 15th day of the third month of it — an election made after that date in the year is treated as made for the following taxable year (IRC § 1362(b))

scorp.distribution.value: a distribution by an S corporation with no accumulated earnings and profits is not included in gross income to the extent it does not exceed the adjusted basis of the stock, and any excess is treated as gain from the sale or exchange of property (IRC § 1368(b))

scorp.fringe_benefits.value: for the fringe benefit provisions the S corporation is treated as a partnership and any 2-percent shareholder as a partner — a 2-percent shareholder being anyone owning, or considered as owning under IRC § 318, more than 2 percent of the outstanding stock or of the total combined voting power on any day of the year (IRC § 1372)

scorp.terminating_election.value: where a shareholder terminates their entire interest during the year and all affected shareholders and the corporation agree, the year is treated as two taxable years the first of which ends on the date of the termination (IRC § 1377(a)(2))

scorp.efile_threshold.value: an S corporation must file Form 1120-S electronically if it is required to file at least 10 returns of any type during the calendar year — there is no longer any asset threshold, and the former 250-return figure was replaced for returns required to be filed on or after 1 January 2024 (Reg. § 301.6037-2(a))

corp.efile_threshold.value: a corporation must file Form 1120 electronically if it is required to file at least 10 returns during the calendar year ending with or within its taxable year, and every member of a controlled group must do so where the group's aggregate is at least 10 — with no asset threshold (Reg. § 301.6011-5(a))

scorp.return_date.value: a calendar-year S corporation files Form 1120-S on or before the 15th day of March following the close of the year, and a fiscal-year S corporation on or before the 15th day of the third month following the close of its year (IRC § 6072(b))

scorp.trusts.value: the trusts that may hold S corporation stock are a wholly grantor trust of a United States citizen or resident; that same trust after the deemed owner dies, but only for the 2-year period beginning on the day of death; a testamentary trust, but only for the 2-year period beginning on the day the stock is transferred to it; a voting trust; an electing small business trust; and, for bank stock only, certain individual retirement accounts (IRC § 1361(c)(2)(A))

scorp.termination.value: an election ends by revocation consented to by shareholders holding more than one-half of the shares — retroactive to the first day of the year if made on or before the 15th day of the 3d month, otherwise from the first day of the following year; by the corporation ceasing to be a small business corporation, effective on the date of cessation; or where the corporation has accumulated earnings and profits at the close of each of 3 consecutive years and more than 25 percent of gross receipts in each is passive investment income, effective the first day of the fourth year (IRC § 1362(d))

llc.separate_entity.value: whether an organization is an entity separate from its owners for federal tax purposes is a matter of federal tax law and does not depend on whether the organization is recognised as an entity under local law (Reg. § 301.7701-1(a)(1))

llc.per_se_corporation.value: a business entity is a corporation for federal tax purposes if it is organised under a federal, State or tribal statute that describes or refers to it as incorporated or as a corporation, body corporate or body politic; if it is an association; if it is a joint-stock company or association, an insurance company, a State-chartered federally insured bank, an entity wholly owned by a State or a foreign government, an entity taxable as a corporation under a Code provision other than IRC § 7701(a)(3), or one of the listed foreign entities (Reg. § 301.7701-2(b))

llc.default_classification.value: unless it elects otherwise, a domestic eligible entity is a partnership if it has two or more members and is disregarded as an entity separate from its owner if it has a single owner (Reg. § 301.7701-3(b)(1))

llc.election.value: an eligible entity with at least two members may elect to be classified as an association, and so a corporation, or as a partnership; one with a single owner may elect to be classified as an association or to be disregarded. The election is made on Form 8832, and is not accepted unless every item the form and instructions require, including the entity taxpayer identifying number, is supplied (Reg. §§ 301.7701-3(a) and (c)(1)(i))

llc.election_effective_date.value: an election takes effect on the date the entity specifies on Form 8832, or on the filing date if none is specified. The date specified may not be more than 75 days before the filing date nor more than 12 months after it; an election specifying an earlier or later date is effective 75 days before, or 12 months after, filing (Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iii))

llc.sixty_month_limit.value: an eligible entity that elects to change its classification may not change it by election again during the 60 months succeeding the effective date, unless the Commissioner permits it because more than 50 percent of the ownership interests at the effective date of the later election are held by persons who held none on the filing date or the effective date of the earlier one. An election by a newly formed entity effective on the date of formation is not a change (Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(iv))

llc.deemed_s_election.value: an eligible entity that timely elects to be an S corporation under IRC § 1362(a)(1) is treated as having elected to be classified as an association, provided it meets the other IRC § 1361(b) requirements as of the effective date — so no separate Form 8832 is needed (Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(1)(v)(C))

llc.employment_tax.value: an entity disregarded for any purpose is nonetheless treated as a corporation for the taxes imposed by subtitle C — chapters 21, 22, 23, 23A, 24 and 25 — so it is the employer of its employees, files the Form 94X series and Forms W-2 under its own name and EIN, and is liable for withholding, FICA and FUTA (Reg. § 301.7701-2(c)(2)(iv)(B))

llc.owner_self_employment.value: the disregarded-entity rule still applies to subtitle A, including chapter 2 self-employment tax, so the entity is not the employer of its own owner; the owner is not an employee and is subject to self-employment tax on the entity activities. The same holds for a partner of a partnership that owns the disregarded entity (Reg. § 301.7701-2(c)(2)(iv)(C)(2))

llc.limited_partner_exclusion.value: in computing net earnings from self-employment there is excluded the distributive share of any item of income or loss of a limited partner, as such, other than IRC § 707(c) guaranteed payments to that partner for services actually rendered to or on behalf of the partnership to the extent established to be in the nature of remuneration for those services (IRC § 1402(a)(13))

exempt.501a.value: an organization described in IRC § 501(c) or (d) or § 401(a) is exempt from taxation under subtitle A unless the exemption is denied under § 502 or § 503, but remains subject to tax on unrelated business income and certain other activities (IRC § 501(a), (b))

exempt.501c3.value: a corporation, community chest, fund or foundation organised and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, public-safety testing, literary or educational purposes, to foster national or international amateur sports competition, or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals; no part of its net earnings inuring to any private shareholder or individual; no substantial part of its activities carrying on propaganda or otherwise attempting to influence legislation; and not participating or intervening in any political campaign for or against a candidate for public office (IRC § 501(c)(3))

exempt.501c4.value: civic leagues or organisations not organised for profit but operated exclusively for the promotion of social welfare, or local associations of employees whose membership is limited to the employees of a designated person in a particular municipality and whose net earnings are devoted exclusively to charitable, educational or recreational purposes (IRC § 501(c)(4)(A))

exempt.501c7.value: clubs organised for pleasure, recreation and other nonprofitable purposes, substantially all the activities of which are for those purposes and no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder (IRC § 501(c)(7))

exempt.508_notice.value: an organisation organised after 9 October 1969 is not treated as described in IRC § 501(c)(3) unless it has given notice to the Secretary that it is applying for recognition of that status, and not for any period before the notice is given if the notice is late (IRC § 508(a))

exempt.508_presumption.value: any organisation described in IRC § 501(c)(3) that does not notify the Secretary that it is not a private foundation is presumed to be one. Neither the notice requirement nor the presumption applies to churches, their integrated auxiliaries and conventions or associations of churches, or to an organisation that is not a private foundation and whose gross receipts are normally not more than $5,000 in each taxable year (IRC § 508(b), (c)(1))

exempt.6033_filing.value: every organisation exempt under IRC § 501(a) must file an annual return stating its items of gross income, receipts and disbursements and such other information as the Secretary prescribes, and must keep records — subject to the mandatory exceptions for churches, their integrated auxiliaries and conventions or associations of churches, the exclusively religious activities of a religious order, and certain listed organisations other than private foundations whose gross receipts are normally not more than $5,000 (IRC § 6033(a)(1), (a)(3))

exempt.epostcard.value: an organisation relieved of the annual return by the gross receipts exception must nonetheless furnish annually, in electronic form, its legal name, mailing and web addresses, taxpayer identification number, the name and address of a principal officer, and evidence of the continuing basis for the exception — and must give notice when it ceases to exist (IRC § 6033(i))

exempt.auto_revocation.value: an organisation that fails to file the annual return or notice for 2 consecutive years is notified by the Secretary; one that fails for 3 consecutive years has its IRC § 501(a) exempt status revoked on and after the due date set for the third return or notice, and the Secretary publishes and maintains a list of the organisations revoked (IRC § 6033(j)(1))

exempt.990_series.value: gross receipts normally $50,000 or less — Form 990-N, with the option of filing a full return instead; gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000 — Form 990-EZ or Form 990; gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or total assets of $500,000 or more — Form 990; a private foundation files Form 990-PF regardless of amount
exempt.990_series.source: IRS, Form 990 series: Which forms do exempt organizations file, page last reviewed 28 June 2026, read at irs.gov/charities-non-profits/form-990-series-which-forms-do-exempt-organizations-file-filing-phase-in

exempt.990n_normally.value: gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less where the organisation has existed 1 year or less and received or was pledged $75,000 or less in its first tax year; has existed between 1 and 3 years and averaged $60,000 or less in each of its first two tax years; or is at least 3 years old and averaged $50,000 or less over the immediately preceding 3 tax years including the year being measured
exempt.990n_normally.source: IRS, Annual electronic filing requirement for small exempt organizations — Form 990-N (e-Postcard), page last reviewed 27 June 2026, read at irs.gov/charities-non-profits/annual-electronic-filing-requirement-for-small-exempt-organizations-form-990-n-e-postcard

exempt.990n_due_date.value: Form 990-N is due by the 15th day of the fifth month after the close of the tax year — 15 May for a calendar-year organisation — and there is no penalty for a late submission, though three consecutive missed years still costs the exemption
exempt.990n_due_date.source: IRS, Annual electronic filing requirement for small exempt organizations — Form 990-N (e-Postcard), page last reviewed 27 June 2026, read at irs.gov/charities-non-profits/annual-electronic-filing-requirement-for-small-exempt-organizations-form-990-n-e-postcard

ubit.tax.value: a tax is imposed for each taxable year on the unrelated business taxable income of every organisation described in IRC § 511(a)(2), computed as provided in IRC § 11 with taxable income read as unrelated business taxable income (IRC § 511(a)(1))

ubit.ubti.value: unrelated business taxable income is the gross income derived from any unrelated trade or business regularly carried on, less the deductions directly connected with carrying it on, both computed with the IRC § 512(b) modifications (IRC § 512(a)(1))

ubit.silo.value: an organisation with more than one unrelated trade or business computes unrelated business taxable income separately for each, including for the net operating loss deduction and without regard to the specific deduction, treating none as less than zero; total unrelated business taxable income is the sum of those amounts less one specific deduction (IRC § 512(a)(6))

ubit.specific_deduction.value: except for computing the net operating loss under IRC § 172 and for the separate computation under IRC § 512(a)(6), a specific deduction of $1,000 is allowed; a diocese, province of a religious order or convention or association of churches is allowed a further deduction for each local unit equal to the lower of $1,000 or that unit gross income from an unrelated trade or business regularly carried on (IRC § 512(b)(12))

ubit.unrelated_trade.value: an unrelated trade or business is any trade or business the conduct of which is not substantially related — aside from the need for income or funds or the use made of the profits — to the exercise of the purpose constituting the basis for exemption. Excluded are a business in which substantially all the work is performed without compensation, one carried on by an IRC § 501(c)(3) organisation or a college or university primarily for the convenience of its members, students, patients, officers or employees, and one that is the selling of merchandise substantially all of which was received as gifts or contributions (IRC § 513(a))

classify.foreign_default.value: unless it elects otherwise, a foreign eligible entity is a partnership if it has two or more members and at least one lacks limited liability; an association if all members have limited liability; and disregarded if it has a single owner who lacks limited liability. Limited liability is determined solely by the statute or law under which the entity is organised, save that where that law lets the entity choose, its organisational documents may also be relevant (Reg. § 301.7701-3(b)(2))

classify.signatures.value: an election must be signed by every member who is an owner when it is filed, or by an officer, manager or member authorised under local law or the organisational documents who represents to that authorisation under penalties of perjury. Where the election is retroactive or changes an existing classification, each person who was an owner during the retroactive period, or on the date the deemed transactions occur, and who is no longer an owner when it is filed, must also sign (Reg. § 301.7701-3(c)(2))

classify.relevance.value: a foreign eligible entity classification is relevant when it affects any person liability for federal tax or information purposes, and the date it becomes relevant is the date of the event creating an obligation to file a return, information return or statement for which the classification must be determined (Reg. § 301.7701-3(d)(1)(i))

classify.relevance_lapse.value: where the classification of a foreign eligible entity has never been relevant, or has not been relevant for 60 consecutive months, its classification is determined afresh under the default rules when it next becomes relevant (Reg. § 301.7701-3(d)(2), (d)(3))

classify.deemed_transactions.value: a partnership electing association status is deemed to contribute all its assets and liabilities to the association for stock and immediately liquidate, distributing the stock to its partners; an association electing partnership status is deemed to distribute all its assets and liabilities to its shareholders in liquidation, who immediately contribute them to a newly formed partnership; an association electing to be disregarded is deemed to distribute all its assets and liabilities to its single owner in liquidation; and a disregarded entity electing association status is deemed to have its owner contribute all its assets and liabilities to the association for stock (Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(1))

classify.step_transaction.value: the tax treatment of a change in classification by election is determined under all relevant provisions of the Code and general principles of tax law, including the step transaction doctrine (Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(2)(i))

classify.plan_of_liquidation.value: for the purpose of the IRC § 332 requirement that a plan of liquidation be adopted, an association making an election to be classified as a partnership or to be disregarded is treated as adopting a plan of liquidation immediately before the deemed liquidation, unless a formal plan contemplating the election was adopted earlier (Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(2)(ii))

classify.timing.value: an election changing a classification is treated as occurring at the start of the day for which it is effective, and the deemed transactions are treated as occurring immediately before the close of the preceding day — so an election effective 1 January puts the deemed liquidation on 31 December, which is the last day of the association taxable year (Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(3)(i))

classify.tiered_order.value: where elections for a series of tiered entities are effective on the same date, the entities may specify the order on Form 8832; if they do not, the deemed transactions occur first for the highest tier entity and then down the chain (Reg. § 301.7701-3(g)(3)(iii))

ein.statutory_hook.value: any person required to make a return, statement or other document must include the identifying number prescribed for securing proper identification, must furnish that number to another person required to show it, and must furnish the number of another person where required (IRC § 6109(a)(1) to (3))

ein.which_number.value: an individual required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number uses a social security number, or an individual taxpayer identification number if not eligible for one; any person other than an individual — corporations, partnerships, nonprofit associations, trusts, estates and similar nonindividual persons — uses an employer identification number (Reg. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(ii)(A) to (C))

ein.sole_proprietor.value: an individual, whether U.S. or foreign, who is an employer or who is engaged in a trade or business as a sole proprietor should use an employer identification number as required by returns, statements or other documents and their instructions (Reg. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(ii)(D))

ein.apply.value: any person required to furnish an employer identification number must apply for one, if not done previously, on Form SS-4, far enough in advance of the first required use to permit issuance in time for compliance (Reg. § 301.6109-1(d)(2)(i))

ein.update.value: a person issued an employer identification number must provide the Service with any updated application information in the manner and frequency required by forms, instructions or other guidance — a requirement applying to every holder of an employer identification number on or after 1 January 2014 (Reg. § 301.6109-1(d)(2)(ii))

ein.responsible_party.value: a responsible party is someone who owns, controls or exercises effective control over the entity and directly or indirectly manages its funds and assets; the application must name one and give their taxpayer identification number, and the responsible party must be a person rather than an entity except for government entities. It is usually the principal officer of a corporation or tax-exempt organisation, a general partner of a partnership, the grantor, owner or trustor of a trust, or the fiduciary of an estate
ein.responsible_party.source: IRS, Responsible parties and nominees, page last reviewed 28 June 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/responsible-parties-and-nominees

ein.nominee.value: a nominee — someone given limited authority to act during formation, with little or no control over the entity assets — cannot apply for an employer identification number and should not be listed on Form SS-4; where a nominee is used for state formation the responsible party must be identified before the application is made
ein.nominee.source: IRS, Responsible parties and nominees, page last reviewed 28 June 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/responsible-parties-and-nominees

ein.daily_limit.value: an applicant may obtain only 1 employer identification number per responsible party per day; the online application must be completed in one session and expires after 15 minutes of inactivity
ein.daily_limit.source: IRS, Get an employer identification number, page last reviewed 19 August 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number

ein.online_eligibility.value: the online application is available only to a domestic organisation formed in the United States or its territories whose principal place of business is there, applied for by the responsible party in control of the entity or an authorised representative holding the responsible party social security number or individual taxpayer identification number; an applicant whose principal place of business is outside the United States must apply by phone, fax or mail
ein.online_eligibility.source: IRS, Get an employer identification number, page last reviewed 19 August 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number

ein.new_sole_proprietor.value: a sole proprietor needs a new employer identification number on incorporating, on forming a partnership, or on declaring bankruptcy, and does not need one on changing the business name or location or on owning multiple businesses
ein.new_sole_proprietor.source: IRS, Do you need a new EIN?, page last reviewed 21 July 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/do-you-need-a-new-ein

ein.new_corporation.value: a corporation needs a new employer identification number on receiving a new charter from the secretary of state, on becoming a subsidiary of another corporation, on changing to a partnership or sole proprietorship, or on merging to create a new corporation — and does not need one on changing name or location, declaring bankruptcy, being a division, surviving a merger, electing S corporation status, reorganising to change only identity or location, or converting at State level without changing structure
ein.new_corporation.source: IRS, Do you need a new EIN?, page last reviewed 21 July 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/do-you-need-a-new-ein

ein.new_partnership.value: a partnership needs a new employer identification number on incorporating, on one partner taking over to operate as a sole proprietor, or on ending a partnership and beginning a new one — and does not need one on changing name or location, declaring bankruptcy, or undergoing a change in ownership that does not terminate the partnership
ein.new_partnership.source: IRS, Do you need a new EIN?, page last reviewed 21 July 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/do-you-need-a-new-ein

ein.new_llc.value: an LLC needs a new employer identification number on terminating and forming a new corporation or partnership, or where a single-member LLC must file excise or employment taxes — and does not need one on changing name or location, reporting as a branch or division of another entity with no employees and no excise tax, converting a partnership to an LLC classified as a partnership, or changing its tax election to a corporation or S corporation
ein.new_llc.source: IRS, Do you need a new EIN?, page last reviewed 21 July 2026, read at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/do-you-need-a-new-ein

ein.section708.value: a new partnership formed as a result of the termination of a partnership under IRC § 708(b)(1)(B) retains the employer identification number of the terminated partnership (Reg. § 301.6109-1(d)(2)(iii))

period.taxable_year.value: the taxable year is the annual accounting period on the basis of which the taxpayer regularly computes income in keeping its books, if that period is a calendar year or a fiscal year; a calendar year is a period of 12 months ending 31 December and a fiscal year a period of 12 months ending on the last day of any other month (IRC § 441(b) to (e))

period.no_books.value: the taxable year is the calendar year where the taxpayer keeps no books, has no annual accounting period, or has one that does not qualify as a fiscal year (IRC § 441(g))

period.52_53_week.value: a taxpayer who in keeping its books regularly computes income on an annual period varying from 52 to 53 weeks, always ending on the same day of the week and always either on the last occurrence of that day in a calendar month or on the occurrence nearest the last day of a calendar month, may elect to compute taxable income on that basis (IRC § 441(f)(1))

period.change_approval.value: a change of annual accounting period makes the new period the taxpayer taxable year only if the change is approved by the Secretary, and a taxpayer to whom IRC § 441(g) applies that adopts an annual accounting period other than a calendar year is treated as having changed its period (IRC § 442)

period.short_period.value: a return for a period of less than 12 months is required where the taxpayer changes its annual accounting period with the approval of the Secretary — running from the day after the close of the former year to the close of the day before the first day of the new year — and where the taxpayer is in existence during only part of what would otherwise be its taxable year (IRC § 443(a)(1), (2))

period.annualisation.value: on a change of annual accounting period the taxable income for the short period is placed on an annual basis by multiplying modified taxable income by 12 and dividing by the number of months in the short period; the tax is the same part of the tax so computed as the number of months in the short period is of 12 months, subject to the relief computation available on application (IRC § 443(b))

period.partnership_required.value: a partnership may not have a taxable year other than the majority interest taxable year; failing that, the taxable year of all its principal partners; failing that, the calendar year unless regulations prescribe another period — save where it establishes a business purpose to the satisfaction of the Secretary, and deferral of income to partners is never a business purpose (IRC § 706(b)(1)(B), (C))

period.majority_interest.value: the majority interest taxable year is the taxable year which, on each testing day, was the taxable year of one or more partners holding an aggregate interest in partnership profits and capital of more than 50 percent, the testing day being the first day of the partnership taxable year or such representative period as the Secretary prescribes. A principal partner is one holding an interest of 5 percent or more in profits or capital, and a partnership required to change under this rule need not change again for either of the 2 following years (IRC § 706(b)(3), (4))

period.s_corporation.value: the taxable year of an S corporation must be a permitted year: a year ending 31 December, or any other accounting period for which the corporation establishes a business purpose to the satisfaction of the Secretary — and deferral of income to shareholders is not a business purpose (IRC § 1378)

period.444_limit.value: a partnership, S corporation or personal service corporation may elect a taxable year other than the required year only if the deferral period of the year elected is not longer than 3 months; where the entity is changing its taxable year, only if that deferral period is not longer than the shorter of 3 months or the deferral period of the year being changed (IRC § 444(b)(1), (2))

period.deferral_period.value: the deferral period of a taxable year is the months between the beginning of that year and the close of the first required taxable year ending within it (IRC § 444(b)(4))

period.444_cost.value: an entity making the election must, if a partnership or S corporation, make the required payments under IRC § 7519, and if a personal service corporation, be subject to the deduction limitations of IRC § 280H. The election remains in effect until the entity changes its taxable year or otherwise terminates it (IRC § 444(c), (d)(2))

period.natural_business_year.value: a natural business year is established by the 25-percent gross receipts test: gross receipts from sales and services for the last 2 months of the 12-month period ending with the last month of the requested year, divided by gross receipts for that whole 12-month period, must equal or exceed 25 percent — and the same computation must do so for each of the two preceding 12-month periods ending with that month. The requested year does not qualify if any other annual accounting period produces a higher average of its three percentages, and a taxpayer without a 47-month history of gross receipts cannot establish a natural business year at all
period.natural_business_year.source: Rev. Proc. 2006-46, read at irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-06-46.pdf, section 5.07

period.business_purpose_deemed.value: the business purpose requirement is generally satisfied, without adjustments to neutralise tax consequences, where the requested annual accounting period coincides with the taxpayer required taxable year, ownership taxable year or natural business year
period.business_purpose_deemed.source: Rev. Proc. 2006-46, read at irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-06-46.pdf, section 2.06

period.no_retroactive.value: unless specifically authorised by the Commissioner, a taxpayer may not request or otherwise make a retroactive change in annual accounting period, whether or not the change is to a required taxable year
period.no_retroactive.source: Rev. Proc. 2006-46, read at irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-06-46.pdf, section 2.03(3)

method.book_conformity.value: taxable income is computed under the method of accounting on the basis of which the taxpayer regularly computes income in keeping its books; where no method has been regularly used, or the method used does not clearly reflect income, the computation is made under such method as in the opinion of the Secretary does clearly reflect it (IRC § 446(a), (b))

method.permissible.value: the permissible methods are the cash receipts and disbursements method, an accrual method, any other method permitted by chapter 1, or any combination of them permitted under regulations (IRC § 446(c))

method.multiple_businesses.value: a taxpayer engaged in more than one trade or business may, in computing taxable income, use a different method of accounting for each trade or business (IRC § 446(d))

method.change_consent.value: a taxpayer who changes the method of accounting on which it regularly computes income in keeping its books must secure the consent of the Secretary before computing taxable income under the new method; the absence of that consent is not taken into account to prevent or reduce any penalty or addition to tax where no request was filed (IRC § 446(e), (f))

method.cash_prohibited.value: a C corporation, a partnership having a C corporation as a partner, and a tax shelter may not compute taxable income under the cash receipts and disbursements method — subject to exceptions for a farming business, a qualified personal service corporation, and an entity meeting the gross receipts test (IRC § 448(a), (b))

method.gross_receipts_2026.value: $32,000,000 — a corporation or partnership meets the gross receipts test for a taxable year beginning in 2026 if its average annual gross receipts for the 3-taxable-year period ending with the preceding taxable year do not exceed that amount. The figure for taxable years beginning in 2025 was $31,000,000, and the unindexed statutory base in IRC § 448(c)(1) is $25,000,000
method.gross_receipts_2026.source: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 § 3.30, read at irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-32.pdf; 2025 figure from Rev. Proc. 2024-40 § 3.31, read at irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-24-40.pdf; statutory base at IRC § 448(c)(1), read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/448

method.gross_receipts_mechanics.value: all persons treated as a single employer under IRC § 52(a) or (b) or § 414(m) or (o) are treated as one person for the test; an entity not in existence for the whole 3-year period applies it over the period it existed; gross receipts for a taxable year of less than 12 months are annualised; gross receipts are reduced by returns and allowances; and a reference to an entity includes any predecessor (IRC § 448(c)(2), (3))

method.economic_performance.value: the all events test is not treated as met any earlier than when economic performance occurs. Where the liability arises out of services or property provided to the taxpayer, economic performance occurs as they are provided; where it requires the taxpayer to provide property or services, as the taxpayer provides them; and where it requires a payment under a workers compensation act or arising out of a tort, as the payments are made (IRC § 461(h)(1), (2))

method.recurring_item.value: an item may be treated as incurred before economic performance where the all events test is otherwise met, economic performance occurs within the shorter of a reasonable period after the close of the year or 8½ months after it, the item is recurring and consistently treated that way, and either the item is not material or accruing it earlier produces a more proper match against income — the treatment on financial statements being taken into account (IRC § 461(h)(3))

method.small_inventory.value: a taxpayer other than a prohibited tax shelter that meets the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test is exempt from the inventory requirement, and its inventory method does not fail to clearly reflect income if it either treats inventory as non-incidental materials and supplies or conforms to the method reflected in its applicable financial statement, or in its books and records prepared under its accounting procedures where it has no such statement (IRC § 471(c))

method.small_263A.value: a taxpayer other than a prohibited tax shelter that meets the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test is exempt from the uniform capitalisation rules, and for a taxpayer that is neither a corporation nor a partnership the test is applied as if each trade or business were a corporation or partnership (IRC § 263A(i))

method.481_adjustment.value: in the year of a change of accounting method there must be taken into account those adjustments determined to be necessary solely by reason of the change, in order to prevent amounts from being duplicated or omitted (IRC § 481(a))

report.6041_threshold.value: $2,000 — every person engaged in a trade or business who pays another person rent, salaries, wages, premiums, annuities, compensations, remunerations, emoluments or other fixed or determinable gains, profits and income of that amount or more in a calendar year must render a return to the Secretary. The figure was $600 until Pub. L. 119-21 § 70433(a) substituted $2,000 for payments made after 31 December 2025, and IRC § 6041(h) indexes it for calendar years after 2026 in multiples of $100 (IRC § 6041(a), (h))
report.6041_threshold.source: IRC § 6041(a), (h) and the 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6041

report.6041a_services.value: a service-recipient engaged in a trade or business that pays remuneration for services in a calendar year must make a return where the aggregate paid to that person equals or exceeds the dollar amount in effect for that year under IRC § 6041(a) — the cross-reference substituted by Pub. L. 119-21 § 70433(c) for the former fixed $600, so the two thresholds now move together (IRC § 6041A(a))
report.6041a_services.source: IRC § 6041A(a) and the 2025 amendment notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6041A

report.6041a_direct_sales.value: $5,000 — a person who sells consumer products to a buyer on a buy-sell, deposit-commission or similar basis for resale other than in a permanent retail establishment must make a return where the aggregate sales to that buyer in the calendar year are that amount or more (IRC § 6041A(b))

report.1099k.value: a third party settlement organisation must report a participating payee third party network transactions only if the amount otherwise reportable exceeds $20,000 and the aggregate number of transactions exceeds 200. Pub. L. 119-21 § 70432(a) restored both tests and did so as if included in the 2021 Act that had replaced them with a flat $600 and no transaction count, so the $600 rule is treated as never having taken effect (IRC § 6050W(e))
report.1099k.source: IRC § 6050W(e) and the 2025 amendment and effective-date notes, read at law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6050W

report.w2.value: every person required to withhold under IRC § 3101 or § 3402, and every employer engaged in a trade or business who pays remuneration for services performed by an employee, must furnish each employee a written statement for the calendar year on or before 31 January of the succeeding year — or, where employment ends before the close of the year, within 30 days after a written request from the employee if that 30-day period ends before 31 January (IRC § 6051(a))

report.due_dates.value: Forms W-2 and W-3 and any return or statement reporting nonemployee compensation are filed on or before 31 January of the year following the calendar year to which they relate; other information returns under subpart B, when filed electronically, are filed on or before 31 March (IRC § 6071(b), (c))

report.efile_threshold.value: no person is required to file information returns electronically for a calendar year unless required to file at least 10 returns during that year, counted in aggregate across return types; a partnership with more than 100 partners must file electronically regardless (Reg. § 301.6011-2(c))

report.8300.value: $10,000 — any person engaged in a trade or business who in the course of it receives more than that amount in cash in one transaction, or in two or more related transactions, must make a return showing the name, address and taxpayer identification number of the person from whom the cash was received, the amount, and the date and nature of the transaction (IRC § 6050I(a), (b))
